newsitem.title: USA: U.S. March employment data points to higher rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. March employment data points to higher rates.

text.p: News that U.S. average hourly earnings rose four percent on a 12-month basis in March along with other signs of strength in the jobs report bolstered the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike near-term, analysts said.
"This is not the definitive blow but it certainly provides supporting evidence for a further hike as early as May," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors.
The four percent increase in average hourly wages was the largest 12-month gain since the 12 months ended June 1990.
On a month-over-month basis, average hourly earnings climbed five cents to $12.15 in March.

Other signs of economic vigor emerged as the Labor Department said the household survey showed 745,000 more people had jobs in March, while the workweek only shrank 0.1 to 34.8 hours. The jobless rate also edged lower to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent in February.

"It's very interesting to see that employment jumped by 745,000 for the month," said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures. "It does reflect the fact that there is a lot of strength in the economy."
Other analysts also warned that certain aspects of the jobs data could portend another increase in short-term rates.
"These are not the kinds of figures to spur a rally (in Treasuries); you can paint a negative side (for bonds)," said Kevin Flanagan, a vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"There was definitive momentum in wages with the highest year-over-year level gains in seven years," Flanagan said.
"Overtime levels are at their highest in 41 years, so it keeps alive and well the notion the Federal Reserve can tighten again on May 20," he added.
Indeed the benchmark U.S. Treasury bond was off 21/32 to yield about 7.13 percent shortly after the employment figures hit the market.

As for the details of the employment report, the economy created 175,000 non-farm payroll jobs in March, which was below the 196,000 gain expected, on average, by economists in a Reuter poll. Overtime hours rose 0.2 to 4.9 in March.
Furthermore, February payrolls were revised lower to post a 293,000 increase versus a previously reported 339,000 rise.
Analysts were careful, however, not to read too much into the fact that the March payrolls gain was less-than-expected and the February increase was lowered.
"Generally, I wouldn't put too much in the downward revision because it was pretty minor," Tainer said. "I wouldn't say that the economy was moderating because of that."
She said the gain of 175,000 in payrolls was understating what was really going on last month in the economy.
Tainer said data going back 15 or 16 years show that the first pass at March payrolls consistently yields "very, very weak" figures; however, revisions typically follow.
